{"id": "ByhDDIlrOPQ", "snippet": {"title": "Greensill: $10bn in Funds and the $440m That Went Elsewhere", "categoryId": "27", "description": "Greensill Capital collapse explained from the regulator, parliamentary and Insolvency Service records.

In November 2020, $440m meant to repay a Credit Suisse fund arrived at Greensill Capital and, the Insolvency Service says, was used for other purposes. Four months later the firm was in administration and $10bn of fund money was frozen. Using FINMA's findings on Credit Suisse, the Treasury Committee and National Audit Office reports, BaFin's order, Lex Greensill's own evidence to MPs, Australian court documents and the 2026 disqualification undertaking, we explain how supply-chain finance turned into future claims on weak borrowers, why one insurance letter mattered so much, and who paid. A disqualification undertaking is not a criminal conviction; the SFO's GFG Alliance investigation is not a finding of guilt.

4:10 The insurance clock

{"id": "Hx17Rhhwn98", "snippet": {"title": "FTX: Customers Got 105% Back. Why He Still Got 25 Years", "categoryId": "27", "description": "FTX collapse explained from the court, SEC and bankruptcy records.

FTX customers have now been repaid 105% of their claims, yet Sam Bankman-Fried is serving 25 years. Using the Second Circuit's June 2026 opinion, the US Attorney's releases, the SEC's complaint, John J. Ray III's sworn bankruptcy declaration, the Delaware bankruptcy court's rulings, the FTX Recovery Trust's distribution notices and the Supreme Court docket, we explain the code privileges, the nine-day run, the trial, the repayments, why claims were fixed at November 2022 prices, and why the courts said repayment does not undo fraud. SEC claims are allegations; the criminal findings are the jury's and the courts'. The Supreme Court has not decided whether to hear his petition.
